title: Complex Escalation
scenario: Mr. Davis, a middle school music teacher, emails the IT Service Desk. His classroom's entire audio system — ceiling speakers, wireless lapel mic, and the wall panel mixer — went completely silent mid-class yesterday. No one reported it yesterday. His choir concert is Friday — three days away. He needs audio restored before then.
impact: Instructional: The choir concert is Friday. A complete audio system failure affecting speakers, wireless mic, and mixer simultaneously suggests a shared upstream cause. The concert deadline makes this time-sensitive despite the late report.
objectives: Verify the scope of the audio failure across all components
Identify the correct escalation path: internal IT vs. vendor support
Gather sufficient evidence so the next team can act without needing to re-investigate
Document the handoff clearly with all relevant context
Follow up with Mr. Davis on restoration status

evidence.description: Photo or description of the mixer display showing current status, input levels, and any error indicators
Documentation of power and cabling checks performed on the mixer, speakers, and wireless mic base station
Vendor ticket number and summary of the escalation, or documentation of the internal fix applied and confirmed

decisionPoints.prompt: All three audio components — ceiling speakers, wireless lapel mic, and the wall mixer — went silent simultaneously. What is the most likely category of failure?

options.label: Vendor hardware failure — one or more components have failed and need repair or replacement
options.feedback: Simultaneous failure of all components points toward a shared cause, possibly the mixer or the upstream power/data feed. Vendor hardware failure is a real possibility and should be investigated.

options.label: User operation error — someone accidentally muted or powered off the mixer or the speakers
options.feedback: Possible, but a simultaneous failure of all three components — including devices Mr. Davis may not have touched — makes this less likely as the sole cause.

options.label: Power issue — a tripped breaker or failed power supply to the mixer or speaker amp has cut power to the entire system
options.feedback: A shared power source failure is consistent with all three components going silent at once. Checking power is a fast and non-destructive first step.

options.label: Software or configuration issue — a firmware update or configuration change to the mixer has disabled outputs
options.feedback: A firmware or config issue could disable outputs, but it typically affects only the mixer, not the wireless mic or passive speakers directly.

decisionPoints.prompt: Internal checks have been completed: power to the mixer is confirmed on, cabling appears intact, and the mixer display shows normal levels. The audio is still not working. At what point do you escalate to the vendor?

options.label: Escalate to the vendor immediately without further internal investigation
options.feedback: Escalating without evidence wastes the vendor's time and may result in a site visit for a simple fix. Gather enough information so the vendor can triage remotely.

options.label: Document mixer settings, cable states, and power checks; escalate to vendor with full evidence
options.feedback: Correct — a well-documented escalation with mixer photos, cable states, and symptoms lets the vendor determine if this is a remote-fixable config issue or requires on-site service, saving time before Friday's concert.

options.label: Order a replacement mixer immediately and swap it out without further diagnosis
options.feedback: Replacing hardware without diagnosis is costly and may not fix the issue if the problem is in the speakers, mic, or cabling rather than the mixer.

ticket.initialDescription: Mr. Davis reports entire classroom audio system silent mid-class. Ceiling speakers, wireless lapel mic, and wall mixer all affected. Choir concert is Friday.

state.display: all inputs nominal, output levels at 0

nodes.title: Review the email
nodes.body: Mr. Davis has emailed the service desk. His entire audio system in Room 215 — ceiling speakers, wireless lapel mic, and wall panel mixer — went silent mid-class yesterday. He did not report it yesterday, and his choir concert is Friday. Acknowledge the email, document the reported symptoms, and open a ticket.

nodes.title: Verify scope and gather history
nodes.body: Ask Mr. Davis clarifying questions: was the audio working before yesterday's class? Did anyone adjust the mixer or move equipment? Did the issue start mid-song or mid-sentence? Check the equipment inventory for the last maintenance date on these devices. Document all findings.

nodes.title: Categorize the failure
nodes.body: All three components went silent at once. Based on the history and symptom pattern, choose the most likely failure category to guide your evidence-gathering approach.

nodes.title: Inspect the audio equipment
nodes.body: Inspect the three audio objects in Room 215: the wall mixer, the wireless mic base station, and the ceiling speakers. For each, record power status, any error indicators, and visible cable conditions. Take a photo of the mixer display. Document all observations.

nodes.title: Check power and cabling
nodes.body: Perform power and cabling checks on all three audio components. Verify the mixer is receiving power, the amp feeding the ceiling speakers is on, and the wireless mic base station is powered. Check that all cables are seated. Document each check and its result.

nodes.title: Determine escalation path
nodes.body: Internal checks are complete. Power is on, cabling appears intact, and the mixer display shows nominal levels. The audio is still not working. Choose the escalation approach that will get the fastest resolution before Friday's concert.

nodes.title: Execute escalation or internal fix
nodes.body: If the issue is vendor-level (hardware failure beyond the mixer), submit a vendor ticket with full documentation: device serial numbers, photos of the mixer display, power/cabling check results, and a summary of symptoms. If the issue has a simple internal fix (e.g., a loose cable, a muted output), apply it and document the change.

nodes.title: Follow up with Mr. Davis
nodes.body: Contact Mr. Davis to give him a status update: what was found, what action is being taken, and the expected timeline for restoration. Given the concert on Friday, set a follow-up reminder to check restoration status before the concert.

nodes.title: Validate restoration
nodes.body: Once the vendor has serviced the equipment or the internal fix has been applied, validate: have Mr. Davis test the speakers, wireless mic, and mixer in a live session. Confirm all three components are working before closing the ticket. Document the validation result with the concert deadline in mind.

nodes.title: Document the ticket
nodes.body: Write a comprehensive ticket summary: what was reported, the timeline (reported one day late), all evidence gathered, the escalation path chosen, the vendor ticket number or internal fix applied, and the validation result. Ensure the next team member can understand the full history without asking Mr. Davis to re-explain.
nodes.prompt: Write an internal ticket note summarizing the audio system failure, the triage and evidence-gathering steps, the escalation decision and vendor ticket details, and the resolution status ahead of Friday's concert.

nodes.title: Debrief
nodes.body: Review your score and identify what to practice next.

kbOpportunity: Simultaneous failure of all audio components in a classroom is often caused by a shared upstream issue — a power failure to the amp, a disabled mixer output, or a vendor-level hardware fault. Always check shared infrastructure before escalating, and document evidence thoroughly so the vendor can triage remotely.
